body: At half past one in the morning a man of twenty-six is walking an aisle in a distribution shed the size of four football pitches, scanning boxes onto a cage. The lighting never changes and neither does the temperature, which is why nobody who works nights can tell you what the weather did. He has one earphone in, which is against the rules and ignored. Somewhere between one aisle and the next it occurs to him that he has not prayed since some point in the spring, and that he does not know exactly when it stopped, and that he does not feel anything much about this either way. He scans the next box.

That is what it usually looks like. Not a crisis, not a rebellion, nothing anybody would think to mention to a pastor. Just a man discovering, at an hour when he is too tired to argue, that he no longer knows what he thinks.

The standard response to a doubting believer is to remove the doubt, usually by supplying an answer at speed. It rarely works, and the reason is that the diagnosis was wrong. Doubt is not a hole in faith. It is very often the shape faith takes in a person who is paying attention.

Consider what faith would even mean without it. Hebrews calls faith the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen, which is a definition built entirely around not having the matter settled. Abraham is commended for going out not knowing where he went, and the not knowing is not an embarrassing detail in that sentence; it is the sentence. Faith is what you do while you are not sure. If you were sure, it would not be faith. It would be arithmetic.

This band carries 121 frequencies, of which teaching and prayer hold a stretch of their own, and every station publishes its schedule before it airs. Not one of them asks a listener to agree with anything before it will play.

That last part is a decision with a price on it. A ministry is rewarded for sounding certain — certainty gathers people, and a station that settles a hard question in eleven seconds will always be shared more widely than one that sits with it. Declining to do that costs listeners. It is done anyway, because the book this band broadcasts from does not do it either. Thomas is offered a hand rather than a rebuke. John the Baptist sends men out of a prison cell to ask whether Jesus is actually the one, and what comes back is a description of what is happening rather than a reprimand for asking. A man says he believes and asks for help with his unbelief in the same breath, and his son is healed regardless.

What has changed is not the amount of doubt in the world but the market for certainty. Confidence is the currency now: the loudest voice in any argument is the one with no visible seam, and the reward for admitting an open question in public is to be treated as unserious. The people selling airtight faith and the people selling airtight departure from it are, structurally, in the same business. Both offer an end to the ache of not knowing, and neither mentions that no such end is available to anybody in this life.

The dial is arranged so a listener can move between registers without announcing anything. There are frequencies where the Word is opened and argued through, for the days when you want that, and ambient and hymn frequencies where nothing is being argued at all, for the days when you could not take it. Nobody has to declare which sort of day it is in order to change stations, which is a small mercy and a rarer one than it should be.
There is a better-intentioned alternative to all of this and it deserves a fair hearing.

It is to answer the question, properly and at once. And the answers do exist: the problem of suffering, the fate of those who never heard, the two passages that appear to contradict each other — every one has a serious literature behind it, written by people who were not frightened, and a good many believers have been rescued by discovering that the objection they thought was fatal has been answered for centuries. The trouble is not the content. It is the timing and the register. An answer delivered at speed tells the person asking that their question alarmed you, and once belief is a series of arguments to be won, every question that does not resolve becomes a defeat rather than a Tuesday.
Every account in Scripture of somebody going badly wrong features a man who was completely sure.

A man of seventy-four is sitting at his own kitchen table at four in the morning with the small lamp on, because the overhead light would be too much. He has taught in that church for forty years and could still take a study on Job at no notice. His wife came home from the hospital on Tuesday with a word in her file that neither of them has said out loud yet. He has the book open at the place he has taught more often than any other, and he is getting nothing from it at all. After a while he stops reading and sits with his hand flat on the page. At about half past five he makes two cups of tea and takes one upstairs, and neither of them mentions it.

Nothing was resolved at that table. He did not arrive at a position, and could not have told you at six whether he had prayed or merely sat still. What he did was stay in the room, and everything that matters in a life of faith is downstream of that.

It would be dishonest to suggest a radio station is any use against the serious version of this. It cannot answer a question, because it does not know you asked one. Doubt of the corrosive kind lasts years, wears people down, and is not touched by a nice arrangement of a hymn. Some of what gets called doubt is exhaustion and some of it is depression, and both need a doctor or a friend who will sit down opposite you for an hour, none of which is available from a transmitter.

But the ache that a broadcast is good for is a real one and it is the commonest of the lot: the ache of having nothing to bring. On the days when you cannot pray, cannot read and would not know what to say if somebody asked, a dial keeps going without your input. It does not check whether you meant it. It plays the psalm whether or not you can join in, and it will still be playing next week when you can. A great deal of the Christian life is simply staying within earshot of something you cannot currently feel.

So doubt is not the opposite of faith. Certainty is, and certainty is the more dangerous condition by a distance: a person who is certain cannot be taught, cannot be corrected, and has no further use for prayer except as a formality. The doubter is still in the conversation. He is asking, which means he still thinks there is somebody there to be asked, and that is not the end of faith. It is the whole working state of it, and the arithmetic will simply have to wait.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. You can move between any of them without explaining yourself to anybody.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 303.10 — Yes and Amen. The name comes from Paul, writing that the promises of God are yes and amen in Christ, and it is worth noticing where the certainty sits in that sentence. It is not in the person listening. Covenant worship is the format that sings what has been settled at the other end — what was promised, by whom, and on whose account it holds — rather than asking a listener to produce a conviction he may not have this week. That makes it the right frequency for a bad Tuesday and for the small end of the night. It does not require you to be sure. It is sure of something on your behalf, and you are allowed to be in the room while it says so.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And there is an account if you want one: it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an argument, since an argument is the last thing that would help. Put HM 303.10 on tonight while you are doing something else, and let it run. You are not required to settle anything by the morning. Faith is what you do while you are not sure, and leaving the radio on is a perfectly respectable thing to be doing while you are not sure.
